newsitem.title: USA: Lockheed, Northrop to merge in $11.6 billion deal.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed, Northrop to merge in $11.6 billion deal.

text.p: Aerospace giant Lockheed Martin Corp. Thursday announced plans to acquire Northrop Grumman Corp. in a $11.6 billion deal, the latest in a series of defence industry mergers in the post-Cold War era.

The deal would create a combined company with 230,000 employees, annual sales of about $37 billion and the firepower to take on aerospace giant Boeing Co., whose $14 billion acquisition of McDonnell Douglas Corp. has been approved in the United States but still faces stiff opposition in Europe.

"Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman have been leaders in consolidating the aerospace industry, and we are now taking the next logical step in combining together to shape the future," said Lockheed Chairman Norman Augustine, who will lead the new Lockheed Martin.
Northrop Chairman Kent Kresa will serve as vice chairman of the merged company.

Lockheed produces the F-16 fighter, the C-130 military cargo plane and the F-117 stealth fighter. Northrop produces the B-2 Stealth bomber, sections of the F-18 fighter jet and a variety of parts for Boeing Co.'s 757, 767 and 777 aircraft.

The deal came as a surprise to industry analysts because Kresa had repeatedly stated that his company is not for sale and has continued growing the company through acquisitions. As recently as May, Northrop bought Logicon Inc. for $740 million.

"Everything that Northrop has bid on in the past couple of years Lockheed has bid on too and so you would have thought if (Lockheed) wanted to do this deal it would have done it a few years ago and taken a competitor out of the market place," said Jon Kutler, an investment banker specialising in the defence industry at QuarterDeck Investment Partners.

Kutler said that while Northrop bought Logicon in May and Westinghouse Electric Corp.'s electronics buisness last year as well as numerous other smaller companies, Lockheed had also bid on many of those companies.
"This is an obvious fit that should have been done some time ago," Kutler said.

Mark Biagetti, an analyst at First Equity, said that the merger of Boeing and McDonnell Douglas Corp. may have been a catalyst for the Lockheed/Northrop deal. With the addition of McDonnell Douglas' military expertise, Boeing is a major competitor to Lockheed in the military fighter aircraft area.
"The McDonnell deal made Boeing significantly stronger there so I think this deal is somewhat in reaction to that," Biagetti said.

Under the deal, Northrop shareholders would receive 1.1923 shares of Lockheed for each share of Northrop. At current stock prices, the merger values Northrop Grumman at about $118 per share, based on early stock activity.

Wall Street traders said the deal could generate intense scrutiny among federal regulators, who this week quashed the proposed $4.6 billion merger of Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc. on antitrust grounds.

However, the Defence Department has been encouraging its suppliers to consolidate, in part because it makes the remaining players more efficient and improves their competitive chances on a global basis.
The latest deal is expected to close by year-end, pending approval by shareholders and regulators.

Relations between Lockheed and Northrop grew closer in May when Northrop joined in Lockheed's bid to build the Joint Strike Fighter. The contract, which is the subject of a head to head battle between Lockheed and Boeing, is regarded as the last mega-contract of the century. The contract to develop and build the planes is worth about $170 billion, but analysts say it could be worth multiples of that when spare parts and services are factored in.
After a delayed opening, Northrop stock soared $21.625 to $110.50 and Lockheed fell $4.75 to $99.25, both on the New York Stock Exchange.

The companies said they hoped to account for the merger as a pooling of interests but might be forced to account for it as a purchase. The effect of the merger will be neutral on 1998 earnings but will add to earnings thereafter, they said.

Lockheed Martin, based in Bethesda, Md., was once 17 separate companies. Over the last 20 years, the aerospace giant acquired the aircraft segments of General Dynamics, creator of the F-16 figther jet and Loral, a group of companies specialising in electronics.
The merger of Lockheed and Martin Marietta in 1995 formed by far the nation's biggest defence contractor, but the proposed merger of McDonnell and Boeing poses a challenge to Lockheed's standing.
Last year, Lockheed Martin led all U.S. defence contractors with $12 billion in prime military contract awards, the second year in a row the aerospace giant has been on top.
Northrop Grumman, based in Los Angeles, was formed by the union of Northrop Corp. and Grumman Corp. in 1994. It employs more than 45,000 people and had 1996 sales of $8 billion.
